questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
questions.explanation: Your heart is a strong muscle. It beats about 100,000 times every day.

questions.question: Which organ do you use to think and remember?
questions.explanation: Your brain sends messages along nerves to every part of your body.

questions.question: Which organs fill with air when you breathe in?
questions.explanation: Air goes in through your nose or mouth and down to your lungs. There, oxygen passes into your blood.

questions.question: What is the name for all the bones in your body together?
questions.explanation: A skeleton holds you up and protects your organs. Muscles pull on it so you can move.

questions.question: How many teeth does a grown-up usually have, wisdom teeth included?
questions.explanation: Grown-up teeth have different shapes for cutting, tearing and grinding food.

questions.question: What is the black circle in the middle of your eye called?
questions.explanation: The pupil is a hole that lets light into your eye.

questions.question: Which tube carries food from your mouth to your stomach?
questions.explanation: It is about 25 centimetres long. Food takes just a few seconds to travel down it.

questions.question: Which bone protects your brain?
questions.explanation: Your skull is made of several bones that grow together as you grow up.

questions.question: Which part of your mouth helps you to taste food?
questions.explanation: Your tongue is covered in tiny bumps. Some of them hold your taste buds.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: Skin covers your whole body. It keeps water in and germs out.

questions.question: Which gas does your body make and breathe out?
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide to make food. They give out the oxygen that we breathe in.

questions.question: What is the joint in the middle of your arm called?
questions.explanation: Your elbow works like a door hinge. It lets your arm bend and straighten.

questions.question: How many sets of teeth do people normally grow in a lifetime?
questions.explanation: Baby teeth fall out from about the age of six. Grown-up teeth must then last for life.

questions.question: What can you feel on your wrist that shows your heart is beating?
questions.explanation: Each pulse is one heartbeat pushing blood through your arteries.

questions.question: What are the tiny holes in your skin called?
questions.explanation: Your skin has millions of pores. Sweat comes out of some, and oil that keeps your skin soft comes out of others.

questions.question: Which two organs clean your blood and make urine?
questions.explanation: Kidneys are shaped like beans. A person can live well with only one.

questions.question: How many main senses do people usually count?
questions.explanation: They are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Scientists count more, such as your sense of balance.

questions.question: Which bones form a cage around your heart and lungs?
questions.explanation: Ribs can move a little, which lets your chest get bigger when you breathe in.

questions.question: Which mineral in milk and cheese helps to build strong bones and teeth?
questions.explanation: Green vegetables such as broccoli also contain calcium.

questions.question: What do we call the little bumps on your skin when you are cold?
questions.explanation: Tiny muscles pull on your hairs. Animals fluff up their fur in the same way to stay warm.

questions.question: What is another name for your backbone?
questions.explanation: Your spine is made of small bones stacked on top of each other. That is why you can bend and twist.

questions.question: What are the tiny living building blocks of your body called?
questions.explanation: Your body has trillions of cells. Different types do different jobs.

questions.question: Where in your body are your biceps?
questions.explanation: The biceps is a muscle that bends your elbow. It bulges when you lift something.

questions.question: Which bag-shaped organ in your belly mixes food with strong juices?
questions.explanation: Your stomach squeezes and churns food into a thick soup. This takes a few hours.

questions.question: What is the salty water that comes from your eyes when you cry?
questions.explanation: Tears also keep your eyes wet and wash out dust every time you blink.

questions.question: What do we call the small, round bone at the front of your knee?
questions.explanation: The kneecap guards your knee joint. Its other name is the patella.

questions.question: What marks on your fingertips are different for every person?
questions.explanation: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

questions.question: What does a doctor use to listen to your heart?
questions.explanation: The doctor puts the flat end on your chest and listens through tubes held at the ears.

questions.question: What does your body make to cool you down when you are hot?
questions.explanation: When sweat dries on your skin, it takes some heat away. That is how you cool down.

questions.question: What is the watery liquid in your mouth that helps you swallow food?
questions.explanation: You make about a litre of saliva a day. It also keeps your mouth clean and moist.

questions.question: What covers the ends of your fingers and toes to protect them?
questions.explanation: Fingernails grow faster than toenails. Both are made of the same tough stuff as hair.

questions.question: Which organ stores urine until you go to the toilet?
questions.explanation: A bladder is stretchy, like a balloon. It tells your brain when it is getting full.

questions.question: What do we call a place where two bones meet?
questions.explanation: Some joints let you move a lot. Others, like those in your skull, hardly move at all.

questions.question: What is the doctor's word for a broken bone?
questions.explanation: Bones can heal by themselves. A cast holds the pieces still while they grow back together.

questions.question: Which tube carries air from your throat down to your lungs?
questions.explanation: The windpipe has rings of stiff cartilage that keep it open, so air can always get through.

questions.question: Which sense tells you that a cat's fur is soft?
questions.explanation: Touch sensors are all over your skin. Your fingertips and lips are extra sensitive.

questions.question: What are the two holes in your nose called?
questions.explanation: Tiny hairs inside your nose catch dust before it reaches your lungs.

questions.question: What happens to your heartbeat when you run fast?
questions.explanation: Your muscles need more oxygen when you run. The heart pumps more blood to bring it.

questions.question: What do we call opening and closing your eyelids quickly?
questions.explanation: You blink about 15 to 20 times a minute. Each blink spreads tears over your eye.

questions.question: What is the thin skin inside your ear that shakes when sound reaches it?
questions.explanation: The shaking passes on through three tiny bones to the inner ear.

questions.question: In which part of the body is the smallest bone?
questions.explanation: The stirrup bone in your middle ear is only about 3 millimetres long.

questions.question: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur is also the strongest bone. It makes up about a quarter of your height.

questions.question: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
questions.explanation: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more room for oxygen.

questions.question: Which vitamin does your skin make when it is in sunlight?
questions.explanation: In northern countries the winter sun is weak. People then get vitamin D from food such as oily fish.

questions.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.explanation: Two small chambers receive blood and two larger ones pump it out.

questions.question: Which large dome-shaped muscle under your lungs helps you breathe?
questions.explanation: When it tightens and flattens, it pulls air into your lungs. Hiccups are sudden jerks of it.

questions.question: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.explanation: Enamel is harder than bone, but acids from sugary food and drinks can wear it away.

questions.question: Which large organ in your upper right belly makes bile to help digest fat?
questions.explanation: The liver also cleans your blood and stores energy for the body.

questions.question: Which blood cells help your body fight germs?
questions.explanation: You have far fewer white blood cells than red ones. Many leave the blood to hunt germs in the body.

questions.question: Which tiny pieces in your blood help it to clot after a cut?
questions.explanation: Platelets stick together and plug the hole. The clot then dries into a scab.

questions.question: Why does food seem tasteless when your nose is blocked?
questions.explanation: Much of what we call flavour comes from smell, which reaches the nose from the back of the mouth.

questions.question: About how much of an adult's body is water?
questions.explanation: Blood and the brain are even more watery. Fat tissue contains less water than muscle.

questions.question: Which hormone from the pancreas helps control the sugar in your blood?
questions.explanation: Doctors in Canada first used insulin as a medicine in 1922, to treat diabetes.

questions.question: Which hormone makes your heart beat faster when you get a fright?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline gets your body ready to run or fight. It is made by two small glands on top of your kidneys.

questions.question: Which hormone, made in the brain when it gets dark, helps you feel sleepy?
questions.explanation: Light makes your brain produce less of it. This is why a dark room helps you sleep.

questions.question: Which layer at the back of the eye turns light into signals for the brain?
questions.explanation: The retina has well over 100 million light-sensing cells.

questions.question: What are the nerve cells of the brain called?
questions.explanation: Neurons send tiny electrical signals to each other. The brain has tens of billions of them.

questions.question: About how many bones does an adult have?
questions.explanation: Babies are born with about 300 soft bones. Many of them join together as the child grows.

questions.question: About how many times a minute does a resting adult heart beat?
questions.explanation: Children's hearts beat faster. Fit athletes often have slower resting heartbeats.

questions.question: Which set shows the four main blood groups?
questions.explanation: The groups depend on markers on red blood cells. Doctors must match them before giving blood to someone.

questions.question: Which pigment gives skin and hair their colour?
questions.explanation: Skin makes more melanin in sunshine, which is why it gets darker.

questions.question: Besides sweet, sour, salty and bitter, what is the fifth basic taste?
questions.explanation: Umami is a savoury taste found in cheese, tomatoes and mushrooms. It was named in Japan in 1908.

questions.question: Which bendy, tough material gives your ears and nose their shape?
questions.explanation: Cartilage also covers the ends of bones in joints, so they slide smoothly.

questions.question: Which tough cords join your muscles to your bones?
questions.explanation: When a muscle pulls on a tendon, the tendon pulls the bone and your limb moves.

questions.question: How many baby teeth does a child have when the full set has grown?
questions.explanation: Babies are born with no teeth showing. The first usually appear at about six months old.

questions.question: In which part of a cell is most of your DNA kept?
questions.explanation: DNA holds the instructions for building your body. The nucleus keeps it safe.

questions.question: Which cell parts are called the powerhouses of the cell?
questions.explanation: They release energy from food. Muscle cells have lots of them because they use so much energy.

questions.question: In which organ does most of the food you eat pass into your blood?
questions.explanation: It is called small because it is narrow, not short. It is much longer than the large intestine.

questions.question: Which side of the body does the left half of your brain mostly control?
questions.explanation: The nerves cross over on their way down, so each half of the brain steers the opposite side.

questions.question: Which bundle of nerves runs inside your backbone?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body.

questions.question: What happens to your pupils when you go into a dark room?
questions.explanation: Bigger pupils let in more light, so you can see better. In bright light they shrink again.

questions.question: Why do you shiver when you are very cold?
questions.correct: Your muscles shake to make heat
questions.explanation: Your brain starts the shivering when your body cools down. Working muscles always make some heat, which is why exercise warms you up too.

questions.question: What stops blood from flowing backwards in your heart?
questions.explanation: The 'lub-dub' sound of a heartbeat is the sound of the valves closing.

questions.question: Which blood vessels carry blood away from your heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries have thick, strong walls because blood is pushed through them with force.

questions.question: When you hit your 'funny bone', what do you really hit?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin at the elbow, so a knock there gives a strange tingling.

questions.question: Which is the largest muscle in the human body?
questions.explanation: Its proper name is gluteus maximus. It moves your thigh and helps you stand up and climb stairs.

questions.question: About how many months does a baby grow before it is born?
questions.explanation: Doctors count a pregnancy as about 40 weeks.

questions.question: What do we call the substances your body makes to find and fight germs?
questions.explanation: Vaccines train your body to make antibodies before you meet the real germ.

questions.question: Having two eyes helps you to judge what?
questions.explanation: Each eye sees from a slightly different angle. The brain compares the two views to work out distance.

questions.question: What do we call an automatic reaction, like pulling your hand from something hot?
questions.explanation: Signals for this reflex take a short cut through the spinal cord, so your body reacts before you have time to think.

questions.question: What are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, where oxygen passes into the blood?
questions.explanation: Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli. Their thin walls let oxygen in and carbon dioxide out.

questions.question: Which part of the brain, at the back, mostly controls balance and smooth movement?
questions.explanation: Cerebellum means 'little brain' in Latin. It sits under the main part of the brain.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are in most human body cells?
questions.explanation: You get 23 from each parent. Egg and sperm cells have only 23.

questions.question: Which Danish scientist won the 1920 Nobel Prize in Medicine for work on how blood reaches working muscles?
questions.explanation: Krogh worked in Copenhagen. He showed that tiny blood vessels in muscles open up when the muscle works.

questions.question: Which Danish doctor won a Nobel Prize in 1903 for treating a skin disease with light?
questions.explanation: He used strong light to treat lupus vulgaris, a kind of tuberculosis of the skin. He founded a light institute in Copenhagen.

questions.question: Which snail-shaped part of the inner ear turns sound into nerve signals?
questions.explanation: Its name comes from an ancient Greek word for snail. Tiny hair cells inside it pick up the vibrations.

questions.question: What are the tiniest blood vessels, where oxygen passes into the body's tissues, called?
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are only one cell thick, so oxygen and nutrients can pass through them.

questions.question: What is the name for the waves of muscle squeezing that push food along your gut?
questions.explanation: It is why astronauts can swallow in space. The muscles squeeze the food along, so gravity is not needed.

questions.question: Hair and nails are mostly made of which tough protein?
questions.explanation: Keratin is also in the top layer of your skin. Animal horns and claws contain it too.

questions.question: About how much of your body's energy does the brain use at rest?
questions.explanation: The brain is only about 2% of your weight, but it uses roughly a fifth of your energy.

questions.question: Which pea-sized gland at the base of the brain is called the 'master gland'?
questions.explanation: It makes hormones that tell other glands what to do. A nearby part of the brain controls it.

questions.question: Where is the eye's blind spot, where you cannot see?
questions.correct: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye
wrong: At the very centre of the retina
Where the lens meets the iris
In the middle of the pupil
questions.explanation: There are no light-sensing cells there. You don't notice it because the brain fills the gap.

questions.question: How many lobes does your right lung have?
questions.explanation: The left lung has only two lobes, which leaves room for the heart.

questions.question: Which thick bundle of nerve fibres joins the two halves of the brain?
questions.explanation: Its name is Latin for 'tough body'. Its hundreds of millions of nerve fibres let the two halves share information.

questions.question: Which part of the brain is vital for forming new memories of facts and events?
questions.explanation: Its name comes from the Greek for 'seahorse', because of its curved shape. There is one on each side of the brain.

questions.question: Which part of the brain, joined to the spinal cord, controls your breathing and heart rate automatically?
questions.explanation: You do not have to think about breathing while you sleep, because the brainstem handles it.

questions.question: Which small, U-shaped bone in the neck does not touch any other bone?
questions.explanation: It holds up the tongue and is held in place by muscles and ligaments.

questions.question: Which is the largest artery in the human body?
questions.explanation: It is about as wide as a garden hose, and it carries blood to nearly the whole body.

questions.question: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood out to the whole body?
questions.explanation: Its wall is thicker than the right ventricle's because it must push blood much further.

questions.question: What is the pale yellow liquid part of blood called?
questions.explanation: Plasma is mostly water and makes up a little over half of your blood.

questions.question: Which is the longest nerve in the human body?
questions.explanation: It runs from the lower back down each leg and is about as thick as your thumb.

questions.question: Which light-sensing cells in the retina let you see colour?
questions.explanation: Cones work best in bright light. Rods work in dim light but see only shades of grey.

questions.question: Which flap closes over your windpipe when you swallow?
questions.explanation: It keeps food and drink out of your windpipe. If something goes down the wrong way, you cough it back up.

questions.question: What is the type of cell division that makes new body cells for growth and repair?
questions.explanation: Meiosis is the other main type. It makes egg and sperm cells.

questions.question: Which blood type is the 'universal donor' for red blood cells?
questions.explanation: O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh markers, so most people's bodies accept them.

questions.question: The enzyme in your saliva starts to break down which food substance?
questions.explanation: Chew a piece of bread for a long time and it starts to taste sweet, because starch turns into sugar.

questions.question: In which soft tissue inside bones are new blood cells made?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow makes millions of new blood cells every second.

questions.question: Which lobe, at the back of the brain, mainly handles what you see?
questions.explanation: Signals from the eyes travel to this area, which turns them into the pictures you see.

questions.question: In the 1660s, the Danish scientist Niels Steensen (Steno) showed that which organ is a muscle?
questions.explanation: Before that, many people believed the heart was the body's heat source. Steno is also famous in geology for his rules about layers of rock.

questions.question: Which vitamin does the body need to help blood clot?
questions.explanation: Danish scientist Henrik Dam named it K, for 'Koagulation', the German word for clotting.

questions.question: What is the outermost layer of human skin called?
questions.explanation: The epidermis constantly renews itself. Its top cells are dead and flake off all the time.

questions.question: What is the clear 'window' at the very front of the eye called?
questions.explanation: The cornea has no blood vessels. While your eyes are open, it takes most of its oxygen straight from the air.

questions.question: What is the small piece of flesh that hangs at the back of your mouth called?
questions.explanation: It hangs from the soft palate, which rises when you swallow to stop food going up into your nose.

questions.question: Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explanation: Most veins carry blood that is low in oxygen. The pulmonary veins are the big exception.

questions.question: Which gland behind the breastbone helps train white blood cells in childhood?
questions.explanation: The thymus is biggest in children and shrinks in adults.

questions.question: Which strong, rope-like protein gives strength to skin, bones and tendons?
questions.explanation: Collagen is the most common protein in the human body. It works like a strong glue holding tissues together.

questions.question: What is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, where much thinking happens, called?
questions.explanation: The folds give the cortex a larger area, so more of it fits inside the skull.

questions.question: What mainly triggers your urge to breathe?
questions.correct: Too much carbon dioxide in the blood
wrong: Too little water in the blood
Too little sugar in the blood
Too little iron in the blood
questions.explanation: A build-up of carbon dioxide tells the brainstem to make you breathe. That is why holding your breath gets harder and harder.

questions.question: About how long does a red blood cell live?
questions.explanation: Old red blood cells are broken down, mostly in the spleen and liver. Their iron is used again to make new ones.

questions.question: The image that forms on the retina is which way up?
questions.explanation: The brain flips the image, so the world looks the right way up to you.
